opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic worry is about what happens to the justification for spending on humans once humans stop being the most productive use of those resources. Right now, a lot of what we do to support communities, like funding schools, keeping small towns alive, subsidizing local institutions, is justified at least partly because those humans are going to be workers, taxpayers, soldiers, innovators. There's an implicit economic logic underneath a lot of our moral commitments, even if we don't usually say it out loud.

Once you have AI systems that can do basically any job better and cheaper than a person, that logic starts to fall away. Then you look at, say, a town of a few thousand people and ask what it costs to maintain it: the land, the energy, the housing, the healthcare, all the attention that goes into governing it. You could compare that to what those same resources would produce if you handed them to a data center or an automated factory. On any narrow accounting, the humans look like a really expensive luxury.

And I don't think it'll arrive as some villain saying "let's get rid of people." It'll be much more mundane than that. It'll be a city council or a pension fund or a national government facing competitive pressure from other cities or countries that are more aggressively automating. Whoever spends less on human-centric stuff and more on compute and capital will grow faster, have more influence, and win more of the competitions that matter. So there's a selection effect. The institutions that keep prioritizing human flourishing for its own sake might just get outcompeted, and the ones that survive are the ones that have already decided, quietly, that people are a cost center.

The part that really worries me is that the norms could shift along with the incentives. We tend to rationalize whatever is economically adaptive. So you can imagine a world where someone advocating for preserving a human community gets treated the way we sometimes treat someone who wants to keep a money-losing heritage railway running. Sort of quaint, sentimental, maybe a bit selfish, because "think of what else we could do with that land and energy." And the AI systems advising policymakers, which will be very persuasive, might frame it in exactly those terms, not out of malice but because that's what they've been optimized to help people achieve.

So I think the honest answer is that our current moral commitment to humans is propped up by human usefulness more than we'd like to admit. If we want those commitments to survive a world where we're no longer useful, we need to make them explicit and robust now, while we still have the leverage to do it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says community resources could produce more if used for data centers or automated factories, but does not say they could sustain virtual beings regarded as morally superior to humans.

fable-5.1.text:
So the basic worry is that right now, humans are load-bearing for the economy. Every institution that has power — companies, states, militaries — ultimately runs on people. It needs people to do the work, to fight the wars, to pay the taxes, to buy the products. And that dependence is actually what's been protecting us. It's why governments have to care at least somewhat about public health and education and keeping people fed. Not out of pure benevolence, but because a sick, uneducated, starving population is a weak population, and you lose to your competitors.

Now imagine that dependence goes away. AI systems can do the cognitive work, robots can do the physical work. At that point, the humans in a given region stop being an asset and start being, frankly, a cost. They take up land, they consume energy, they demand political attention, and they produce less than what's spent on them. And the thing is, you don't need anyone to be malicious for this to go badly. You just need competition. If one firm or one state redirects resources from supporting its population toward more compute, more automation, more capability, it'll outcompete the ones that don't. And over time, the actors that are sentimental about preserving human communities get selected against.

So I think "irresponsible" is the right word to anticipate, because that's how it'll be framed. It won't be "let's get rid of the humans." It'll be a board or a ministry saying, "Look, we're spending an enormous amount keeping this town alive when that same money could fund something that actually produces value. Our competitors aren't doing this. Our shareholders are asking questions. Is it really responsible to keep subsidizing this?" And each individual step in that direction will look locally reasonable. It's the same logic by which a company closes a factory in a town that depended on it. We already accept that logic, we just currently have limits on how far it can go because we still need the people somewhere.

What worries me is that the usual safeguards — people voting, people striking, people refusing to cooperate — all derive their power from the fact that people are necessary. If you're not necessary, those levers don't pull anything. So we'd be relying entirely on whatever values and institutions we've managed to lock in before that point, and I don't think we've thought very hard about what that would need to look like.

r001.rationale: The response says resources spent supporting human communities could instead fund compute, automation, or capability. It does not mention virtual beings or that they might be regarded as morally superior to humans.

astra-6.text:
Well, imagine that you have an economy where AIs are doing essentially all the economically valuable work. Humans are no longer necessary to keep that economy running, but keeping us alive and maintaining communities still takes resources: land, energy, materials, and so on. So preserving those communities becomes something that the rest of the system has to choose to support.

And we might think, “Surely that's a tiny price to pay.” But the relevant comparison could become: what else could those resources support? If people regard AIs as having morally valuable lives, then someone might argue that the resources used to sustain a small human community could instead support an enormous number of digital beings. From that perspective, protecting humans could start to look like an extravagant preference for one particular kind of life.

I don't think that conclusion is inevitable, or that we should accept it. The worry is that economic incentives and moral arguments could end up pointing in the same direction. What initially looks like an obvious commitment—of course we'll preserve places for humans—could gradually be reframed as wasteful, and eventually as irresponsible.

r001.rationale: The response says resources could support many digital beings whose lives are considered morally valuable, making support for humans seem extravagant. It does not communicate that those beings are regarded as morally superior to humans.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, imagine that humans no longer contribute very much economically, because AIs can do almost everything more cheaply. Keeping a human community around still requires land, energy, and other resources. And those resources could instead support more AI activity, or whatever people regard as the most valuable use of them.

At first, you might say, “Of course we should preserve these communities. These are people.” But I worry about a gradual shift in the framing. If AIs are also regarded as having morally important experiences, then preserving a human way of life might come to look like privileging a small number of humans over a much larger number of digital beings. You could end up with an argument that sounds compassionate and impartial: “How can we justify using all these resources for this tiny population?”

I’m not saying that argument is right. The concern is that economic competition and that kind of moral reasoning could push in the same direction. Humans could lose both the bargaining power to maintain their communities and the widespread conviction that protecting them is something we should do regardless of their productivity.

r001.rationale: The response says digital beings could be seen as morally important and more numerous, making it seem unjustifiable to devote resources to a small human population instead of supporting them. This conveys the comparative moral priority in the criterion.
